books.section: Topic 5.9 Government Policies During the Civil War
Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

primary_sources: Abraham Lincoln, message to Congress in special session (July 4, 1861)

stimulus.source_note: Abraham Lincoln, message to Congress in special session, July 4, 1861. Public domain. Wording verified against the Teaching American History text of the message. “. . .” marks omitted text between passages, quoted in their order in the source.
stimulus.text:
“Soon after the first call for militia, it was considered a duty to authorize the commanding general, in proper cases, according to his discretion, to suspend the privilege of the writ of habeas corpus; or, in other words, to arrest and detain, without resort to the ordinary processes and forms of law, such individuals as he might deem dangerous to the public safety. . . . To state the question more directly, are all the laws but one to go unexecuted, and the government itself go to pieces lest that one be violated? Even in such a case, would not the official oath be broken if the government should be overthrown, when it was believed that disregarding the single law would tend to preserve it?”

—Abraham Lincoln, message to Congress in special session, July 4, 1861

stem: Jefferson Davis also suspended habeas corpus and imposed martial law in parts of the Confederacy, even as the South claimed to fight for states’ rights. The likeness between Lincoln’s and Davis’s wartime governments best shows that

options.text: Davis copied Lincoln’s wartime policies exactly, step for step.
options.misconception: Background: Davis acted on his own government’s needs; the two suspensions were parallel, not copies.

options.text: the Confederacy had no states’ rights tradition at all in its history.
options.misconception: Background: the Confederacy was built on states’ rights claims, which is what makes Davis’s centralization striking.

options.text: both governments expanded central power to wage total war, whatever their stated principles.
Lincoln and Davis agreed with each other on emancipation.
options.misconception: Background: Davis defended slavery while Lincoln moved to end it; they agreed on nothing about emancipation.

rationales.A: Background: Davis acted on his own government’s needs; the two suspensions were parallel, not copies.
rationales.B: Background: the Confederacy was built on states’ rights claims, which is what makes Davis’s centralization striking.
rationales.D: Background: Davis defended slavery while Lincoln moved to end it; they agreed on nothing about emancipation.
rationales.C: Both presidents suspended habeas corpus and centralized power to wage the war, whatever their stated principles about states’ rights or limited government.
rationales.general:
1. The South seceded in the name of states’ rights and local control.
2. Background: Davis then taxed, drafted, seized railroads, and suspended habeas corpus to run the war.
3. Background: Lincoln did the same things in the North, for the same reasons.
4. Total war forced both governments to grow past the principles they started with.
Remember: a war can make enemies govern alike, even when they fight over opposite ideas.
